items.title: Matty Matheson's Maker Pizza Picks a 31-Storey City Centre Condo for Its Next Location
items.summary: According to INsauga, Maker Pizza, the fast-growing Toronto pizza chain co-founded by celebrity chef Matty Matheson, is set to open its second suburban location inside Mississauga's Exchange Signature Residences, a 31-storey condo tower near Square One. The chain's first suburban outpost opened in Thornhill, and INsauga reports the Mississauga location will sit inside the Exchange District, a new residential development in the City Centre neighbourhood. A countdown on Maker Pizza's website points to an opening in just over three weeks, following an announcement the company made earlier this summer. The exact menu for the Mississauga location hasn't been released yet, but INsauga notes the chain is known for slices like the truffle shuffle, a bechamel-based pie called Frank's Best, and a chili-pineapple Tropic Thunder pizza, alongside a classic cheese pie. Beyond pizza, the restaurant also serves chicken wings and garlic fingers. For Mississauga's City Centre, the opening adds another dining option to a neighbourhood already anchored by Square One and its growing cluster of condo towers.

items.title: Council Renames a Ward 3 Park to Mark Mississauga's New Sister-City Ties With Ternopil
items.summary: According to Mississauga.com, city council voted at its July 29 meeting to rename Gulleden Park, located at 3570 Havenwood Dr. in Ward 3, to Ternopil Park. The change honours the sister-city partnership Mississauga formally entered with Ternopil, Ukraine, earlier this year. Mississauga.com reports the site was chosen partly because of its proximity to St. Sofia Byzantine Catholic Elementary School, which runs a Ukrainian bilingual program, and to a neighbourhood home to many residents of Ukrainian heritage. Mayor Carolyn Parrish said in a news release that the renaming is a meaningful symbol of the friendship between the two cities and the ties being built through the partnership. This marks only the second Mississauga park named after a sister city, following Kariya Park, which opened in 1992 to mark the city's relationship with Kariya, Japan. The gesture reflects how Mississauga uses its public spaces to formally recognize its international community partnerships.

items.title: Waterloo Police Charge a 57-Year-Old Mississauga Man After a Fatal Ibogaine Ceremony
items.summary: According to INsauga, Waterloo Regional Police have charged 57-year-old Luis Da Silva of Mississauga with criminal negligence causing death and recklessly selling a prescription drug, following the death of a man who took part in a private healing ceremony. Police say their General Investigations Unit opened a sudden death investigation on July 4 after the man, who had arranged to take part in an ibogaine healing experience, died. INsauga reports ibogaine is a psychoactive alkaloid drawn from the root bark of a shrub native to Central West Africa, and that Health Canada has not approved it as a medical treatment or authorized its use in the country. As part of the investigation, police raided a residence in Mississauga on July 30 and seized suspected ibogaine along with several other powders, liquids and capsules, which have been sent to Health Canada for analysis. Investigators have not released where the healing ceremony took place or confirmed the identity of the man who died. The case remains under investigation while authorities wait on the results of Health Canada's analysis of the seized substances.

items.title: A 200-Year-Old Streetsville Log Cabin Traces Back to the Family Behind Toronto's Leslieville
items.summary: According to INsauga, Toronto's Leslieville neighbourhood takes its name from George Leslie, one of the sons of a family that once lived in what is now Mississauga's Leslie Log House. The book Leslieville, written by Joanne Doucette and published in 2016, documents how the Leslie family sailed from Scotland to Canada in 1825, landing in Quebec in mid-May, before John Leslie travelled ahead alone to a property in what was then Toronto Township. INsauga reports John Leslie, his wife Esther Beattie Leslie, and their children later built and lived in the log house on land the family leased, and eventually purchased, from King's College, keeping the property in the family for a century. The home was originally built just north of Derry Road in Meadowvale before being relocated in 1994 to its current site at 4415 Mississauga Rd. in Streetsville. Built in 1826, the log house is one of the oldest surviving log homes in Ontario and holds designated heritage status, with the city marking its 200th anniversary this past weekend. The connection means a piece of east Toronto's identity traces directly back to a family whose original homestead still stands in present-day Mississauga.

items.title: Crews Are Hand-Spraying Individual Plants Along Etobicoke Creek Trail to Fight a Skin-Burning Invader
items.summary: According to INsauga, the City of Mississauga began a targeted herbicide application on Wednesday, August 5, to control wild parsnip along the Etobicoke Creek Trail. Wild parsnip is an invasive plant not native to Ontario, and its sap can cause severe skin reactions when exposed to sunlight, leading to painful burns, while contact with the eyes can cause serious injury including blindness. INsauga reports crews are using VisionMax, a glyphosate-based product, applied with handheld and backpack sprayers so individual plants can be treated directly rather than spraying the area broadly, a method meant to limit impact on surrounding vegetation. Ward 3 Councillor Chris Fonseca alerted residents to the upcoming work along the trail ahead of the application. Left unchecked, the plant spreads quickly through sunny areas like trails, roadsides, shorelines and forest clearings, and dense patches can crowd out native species and disrupt local ecosystems. The targeted approach reflects an attempt to balance public safety concerns around the plant itself with the usual concerns residents raise whenever herbicide is used in public spaces.

items.title: Loose Screens and Balcony Furniture Are Bigger Fall Risks Than Most Residents Realize, City Warns
items.summary: According to the City of Mississauga, falls from windows and balconies can cause serious injury or death, though the city says many of these incidents are preventable through simple precautions under its Balcony Basics awareness campaign. The city identifies common hazards as furniture placed too close to windows or balcony railings, windows left unsecured, and screens that were never designed to stop a fall in the first place. Young children face the highest risk, while older adults can be more vulnerable because of mobility or balance issues, the city says. Renters and highrise residents are encouraged to learn how to recognize these hazards themselves and report concerns early rather than waiting for something to go wrong. The responsibility doesn't stop with tenants. The city says property owners, landlords and building managers must also keep safety features in working order and respond quickly once a problem is flagged. Mississauga backs up the campaign with education, inspections and enforcement action aimed at preventing injuries before they happen.

items.title: Peel's Colour-Coded Health Inspection System Just Played Out at a Mississauga Restaurant
items.summary: According to INsauga, Peel Public Health records show that Charminar Indian Cuisine on Spectrum Way in Mississauga received a red card during an inspection on July 31, the most serious rating the agency issues. Inspectors found what the report describes as a significant risk of possible contamination or adulteration at the restaurant, serious enough to trigger an immediate closure. INsauga explains that a red card means an inspector found an actual health risk or danger, and under Peel's system that forces the establishment to close until the problem is fixed. Charminar has since been reinspected and given a green passing grade, allowing the restaurant to reopen. The outlet also notes the distinction with a yellow card, which signals a conditional pass where the establishment isn't fully meeting requirements under the Health Protection and Promotion Act but can keep operating while it fixes the issues. For Charminar's customers, the sequence shows how quickly a serious violation can shut a kitchen down, and how a passed reinspection gets it back open just as fast.
